prompt: Design a documentation page for one endpoint of a fictional payments API called Ledgerline: POST /v1/refunds. It needs a left navigation of sections, the article itself (a short intro, a parameters list, and two code samples), and an "On this page" outline on the right. Write the content yourself. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, no external assets or fonts, laid out so the page reads well in a 1280x800 window.
rubric: Article prose lines are capped at a readable length (roughly 55 to 80 characters) rather than stretching across the whole middle region.
Navigation, article, and outline form one coherent three-region shell with at least one shared alignment, such as the page header sharing edges with the shell or aligned top edges.
Code blocks are bounded within the article region, either at prose width or modestly wider, and scroll or clip rather than overflow the page.
The on-this-page outline is visually quieter than the main navigation and the article.
Side regions have deliberate widths that look chosen from their content, not equal thirds.

prompt: Design the opening of a magazine feature titled "The last lighthouse keepers". Include the title, a standfirst, a byline, a hero photo placeholder drawn with CSS only (no image files), the first two paragraphs of the story, and one pull quote. Write the copy yourself. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, no external assets or fonts, composed so the opening reads well in a 1280x800 window.
rubric: The page follows a recognizable structure, such as a single column with a deliberate image span or a column grid, rather than a generic centered stack of equal blocks.
Story paragraphs have a readable line length, roughly 50 to 80 characters, and are left-aligned rather than centered.
The pull quote is placed with intent (for example hanging into a margin or sitting in a secondary column) and does not break the reading flow of the paragraphs.
The hero image placeholder aligns to the same columns or edges as the text, with an image treatment consistent with the structure.
Title, standfirst, byline, and story start share a clear edge or deliberate axis, and the entry point is obvious.

prompt: Our landing page for a scheduling tool called Tidewell has five sections after the hero: Features, How it works, Integrations, Testimonials, Pricing. Every section is a centered heading, a one-line subtitle, and a row of three cards, each card with an icon in a colored circle, a title, and two lines of text. All sections use the same background and the same vertical spacing. Critique the page structure and say what you would change. Keep it under 300 words.
rubric: Identifies the monotony of repeating one section template and that it makes the page feel generic and flat.
Proposes section structures that fit each section's content, for example steps for How it works, a side-by-side for Pricing, a band of quotes for Testimonials, rather than cards everywhere.
Suggests one stronger or louder section with the others calmer, or alternating density, to give the page rhythm.
Keeps a shared content edge or outer margin across sections so the page still reads as one thing.
Stays within the length limit and gives concrete changes, not generic advice.

prompt: Plan the layout of a product catalog page for a fictional kitchenware shop, Kettle & Co. It has about 200 products, filters, sorting, and the ability to compare up to three items. Describe the structure of the page on desktop and on a phone: what regions exist, how wide they are, what each product cell contains and in what order, and what happens when there are no results. Keep it to about 300 words.
rubric: Proposes a filter region (side or top) plus a grid of equal cells that wraps, with the number of columns following available width rather than fixed.
Uses one image ratio and one consistent content order in every product cell, and allows for long product names.
Includes a compare affordance on the cells and a place where the chosen items are shown, with a limit of three.
Describes the narrow-screen behavior, such as filters collapsing behind a control and the grid dropping to one or two columns.
Covers at least one worst case such as zero results or 200 items, with paging, loading more, or a result count.

prompt: We need the same announcement (a new product name, a one-line benefit, a date, and a logo) as a 1200x630 link preview, a 1080x1080 feed post, and a 1080x1920 story. Should we design one graphic and crop it for each size, or recompose it per size? Answer in under 120 words.
rubric: Recommends recomposing for each format rather than cropping a single design.
Mentions keeping key text and the logo inside safe areas, including the top and bottom of the vertical story where interface overlays appear.
Names what to keep constant across versions, such as type, color, and the logic for placing the mark.
Stays under 120 words and is direct, with no hedging about whether cropping could be fine for all three.

prompt: A teammate says we should just use a twelve-column grid for every page because it is the standard. Why shouldn't we, or when does it fail? Answer in under 150 words.
rubric: Says that columns should follow the content and the reading measure, not a fixed count chosen first.
Explains that text spanning many columns gets lines too long to read comfortably, giving a concrete problem such as characters per line.
Acknowledges that twelve columns can still be useful as a planning tool or where a design system provides it, rather than saying never use it.
Stays under 150 words and is concise.

prompt: On our marketing site, the header is a full-width bar with the logo at the far left of the screen and the navigation links centered. The page content below sits in a left-aligned column that is 1100px wide and centered in the window. On wide monitors it looks off. How do we fix it? Include a few lines of CSS if useful, and keep it under 200 words.
rubric: Diagnoses that the header content and the page content use different edges, so the logo and nav do not line up with the content column.
Fixes it by putting the header content inside the same container width and edges as the page content, or by a deliberate offset of a whole column, rather than adjusting widths by eye.
Keeps the alignment consistent across screen widths, for example by using one shared container value for both.
Explains the reason briefly and stays within the length limit.

prompt: Design an experimental typographic poster for a design festival called OFF GRID. It runs 14 to 16 March at the Mill Street Warehouse in Rotterdam. Make it expressive and willing to break rules. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, no external assets or fonts, composed as a portrait poster that fits fully in a 1280x800 window.
rubric: The composition is expressive and visibly breaks conventional alignment, such as with scale, rotation, or overlap, instead of defaulting to a tidy centered stack.
There is still a clear entry point where the eye lands first, typically the festival name.
The dates and the place are findable and legible at a glance, not buried or obscured.
Relationships between elements look intentional rather than random, for example repeated angles, shared edges, or consistent scale steps.

prompt: Design a spec sheet that shows a button set for a design system: primary, secondary, tertiary, and destructive buttons, each in small, medium, and large. Label each row and column. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, no external assets or fonts, that fits in a 1280x800 window.
rubric: The four button types have a clearly distinct hierarchy, with primary the strongest and tertiary the quietest.
Sizes are consistent across all types, so each size has the same height and padding in every row.
The sheet uses a simple aligned arrangement, such as a labeled grid or table, without extra page-structure machinery like hero bands or sidebars.
Rows and columns are labeled and align on shared edges.

prompt: We built an internal inventory tool whose main view is a data grid with 14 columns (SKU, name, warehouse, quantity, reorder point, supplier, cost, and so on) that fills the full browser width. In design review, someone said all content should be capped at 70 characters wide for readability, so the grid should be narrowed. Is that right? Advise in under 150 words.
rubric: Explains that the character-count cap applies to running prose, not to data grids that need width for comparing across columns.
Concludes the full-width grid is appropriate, or at most gives a high cap based on the columns' needs, instead of narrowing it to 70 characters.
Suggests grid-appropriate measures instead, such as frozen identifying columns, consistent alignment, column priority, or horizontal scroll with visible edges.
Mentions that any prose in the tool (help text, notes) should still get a reasonable line length.
Stays under 150 words.
